questions.q: What is Meridian Outdoor Supply, as used in this lesson's case study?
options: A real company whose actual Power BI data is shown in this lesson
A fictional, illustrative company invented to walk through this course's concepts applied together
A real Microsoft customer named in their public case studies
The name of a Power BI feature
questions.explain: Meridian Outdoor Supply is explicitly a fictional, illustrative composite used to walk through this course's lessons as one connected scenario — not a real company or real data.

questions.q: What was Meridian's core problem at the start of the case study?
options: Their Power BI tenant had too few workspaces
Three regional managers each built their own version of the same report, producing three different numbers for the same metric
Their reports were too slow to load
They had too many certified datasets
questions.explain: Three competing, slightly different copies of the same 'Weekly Sales Flash' report produced three different revenue numbers at the same leadership meeting, with no way to tell which to trust.

questions.q: Why did the fix start with consolidating workspaces rather than immediately certifying one of the existing reports?
options: Because certification was unavailable to this organization
Because certifying one of three competing, duplicate copies wouldn't fix the underlying problem of three different sources existing at all
Because consolidation is required before anyone can create a workspace
There was no particular reason — the order was arbitrary
questions.explain: Certifying one of three duplicate, inconsistent copies wouldn't address the root cause — the fix had to start by reducing three competing sources down to one owned, governed source.

questions.q: What did impact analysis catch during Meridian's later schema change, according to the case study?
options: Nothing — impact analysis wasn't used in this scenario
That the change would silently break four downstream reports across two workspaces, including one the CFO used weekly
That the change would delete the entire dataset
That the change required a new Power BI Premium license
questions.explain: Before the schema change shipped, impact analysis revealed it would have silently broken four downstream reports — letting the team fix the dependent measures before anyone was affected.

questions.q: How did the schema change actually reach the production report everyone used, according to the case study?
options: It was applied directly to production with no testing
Through a deployment pipeline — built in Development, validated in Test, then deployed to Production
By emailing a new .pbix file to everyone
It never reached production at all
questions.explain: The change moved through a real deployment pipeline — Development, then Test for validation, and only then Production — rather than being applied directly as a shortcut.
